item.text: {"question_id":"6B.8","answer":"During López Obrador’s 2023 period, Mexico had substantial formal rights and dignity protections, including nationwide same-sex marriage, simplified gender-marker recognition in 21 states, disability-rights reforms, older-persons treaty ratification, and IMSS-BIENESTAR rules requiring equal, confidential, informed-consent-based, dignified and non-discriminatory care with complaint channels. These measures were generally enacted by Congress, courts, autonomous institutions, federal agencies, or international partnerships, so personal presidential authorship is limited. Implementation and practical remedy remained inadequate: accessibility materials and technical capacity were insufficient; discrimination affected people with disabilities and Indigenous people; Indigenous, migrant, child, and psychosocially disabled persons faced discriminatory or arbitrary detention; gender-violence investigations remained marked by impunity and victim revictimization; and legal remedies such as amparo rarely produced immediate release. Disaggregated indicators also showed persistent opportunity gaps for Indigenous women, women in poverty, people with disabilities, rural and Indigenous children, and other disadvantaged groups. The evidence therefore supports real formal protections and some institutional remedy, but not reliable equal dignity or effective enforcement in everyday life; national averages cannot offset these group-specific
